questions.explain: External scripts are off by default; the chapter shows enabling via sp_configure 'external scripts enabled', 1 followed by RECONFIGURE, noting a service restart is required for it to take effect.
options: Installing Python for Windows on the database server is sufficient; execution is on by default
EXEC sp_configure 'external scripts enabled', 1; RECONFIGURE; and a SQL Server service restart
Creating a database-scoped credential and granting CONTROL SERVER to the Launchpad account
Enabling the 'Python for SQL Server' feature in SSMS under Server Properties
questions.q: What is required to enable SQL Server Machine Learning Services for in-database Python/R execution?

questions.explain: Because external runtimes run outside SQL Server's memory manager, the chapter creates an EXTERNAL RESOURCE POOL (e.g., MAX_CPU_PERCENT = 40) so a runaway Python job doing a large in-memory join cannot starve the relational engine.
options: To reserve tempdb space for the Launchpad service's scratch files
Python scripts cannot use Windows authentication, so the pool isolates their security context
The pool is required for the model registry table dbo.ml_models to function
External scripts run outside the SQL Server memory manager, so an unconstrained Python process can push the OS into paging and take down the whole instance
questions.q: Why does the chapter insist on constraining ML Services with a dedicated external resource pool?

questions.explain: Persisted memory grant feedback (2022+) lives in Query Store, so it survives restarts and plan cache evictions, and the chapter diagnoses it by querying sys.query_store_plan_feedback joined to Query Store plan views.
options: Cardinality estimation (CE) feedback, introduced in SQL Server 2019
Degree of parallelism (DOP) feedback
Parameter sensitive plan (PSP) optimization
Persisted memory grant feedback (SQL Server 2022+) with state recorded in sys.query_store_plan_feedback
questions.q: Which Intelligent Query Processing feedback feature is persisted in Query Store and survives restarts and plan cache evictions?

questions.explain: Feedback oscillation is the flap cycle described in the chapter — a grant change alters the plan, which invalidates the feedback, which re-learns — and the fix is to stabilize one side: force the known-good plan with sp_query_store_force_plan or turn off the feedback at database scope while investigating.
options: When two memory grant adjustments cancel each other out; fix by restarting the Launchpad service

When feedback increases a grant, changing the plan choice, invalidating the feedback, and re-learning in a cycle; stabilize by forcing the last-known-good plan with sp_query_store_force_plan or disabling the specific feedback via ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION
When DOP feedback and CE feedback disagree on plan choice; fix by enabling Automatic Tuning
When Query Store flushes feedback too aggressively; fix by increasing the Query Store capture interval
questions.q: What is 'feedback oscillation' in Intelligent Query Processing, and how does the chapter recommend stabilizing it?

questions.explain: The chapter's contract: PREDICT applies the VARBINARY(MAX) ONNX model row by row, so put the WHERE clause on the driving table before the CROSS APPLY, remember ONNX scoring is CPU-bound, version models in the registry table, and use the Lambda-style pre-compute pattern for large batches.
options: The model is loaded once per database startup and cached in the plan cache for all sessions
PREDICT only supports models trained inside sp_execute_external_script

The model runs on every row the query touches, so filter before you score (WHERE on the driving table, not after the CROSS APPLY); it is CPU-bound, so reserve it for filtered interactive sets and pre-compute large batches
The .onnx file must be re-uploaded with OPENROWSET before every query execution
